How Nav Mode, Ctrl and app shortcuts work together

Nav Mode turns letter keys into navigation and shortcut keys. The result can differ by app because some apps understand Android editor actions, while others only react to real Ctrl shortcuts.
Ctrl-hold navigation When Ctrl-hold navigation is off, physically held Ctrl is passed to the app whenever possible. Shortcuts such as Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, or Ctrl+Z can then work directly in editors.
When Ctrl-hold navigation is on, physically held Ctrl first uses the Nav Mode mappings below. A mapped key performs its configured Nav Mode command.
Double-tap Ctrl Double-tapping Ctrl latches Nav Mode. After that, pressing a letter triggers the Nav Mode mapping until Nav Mode is left again. This is useful for arrows, Page Up/Down, Escape, Tab, and selection commands without holding Ctrl.
Action vs. Native Ctrl Actions such as Copy, Paste, Cut, Select All, and Undo are sent as Android editor actions. They work in many text fields, but not every app supports every action.
Use Native Ctrl when an app expects a real shortcut. For example, mapping I to Native Ctrl sends Ctrl+I, so editors such as Google Docs can use it for italic text. Undo can also be mapped as Native Ctrl if an app handles Ctrl+Z better than Android Undo.
QWERTZ on physical QWERTY Nav Mode uses the physical key position so navigation remains stable. Layout hints on keys show when the active text layout would treat that physical key as a different letter, such as Y/Z on QWERTZ.
Layout-aware app Ctrl shortcuts When held Ctrl is passed to apps, this optional setting can translate Ctrl+letter through the active Numen layout first. It affects app shortcuts, not the physical Nav Mode grid.
Overrides Each key can be configured as Keycode, Action, Native Ctrl, or None. Use overrides to solve app-specific conflicts without changing the whole mode.

There are two paths for held Ctrl. If Ctrl-hold navigation is on, Numen handles Ctrl+key with the Nav Mode mappings shown below. If Ctrl-hold navigation is off, Numen passes Ctrl+key to the app. This option only affects that app path: when enabled, Ctrl+letter is translated through the active Numen layout first, so shortcuts can follow the letters you type. When disabled, apps receive the original physical key positions.

Numen continues as Numen

Numen 0.86 is the final planned Numen release with new features. You can keep using Numen; security-relevant issues will continue to receive updates. Numen continues the project with the same principles and remains free, open-source software under the GPLv3 copyleft licence. When Numen is ready, Numen will notify you and guide you through the one-time transfer of your settings.
Numen fits the keyboard bar to the Elite’s rounded display.

Enable Numen
To get started, you need to enable Numen as an input method in Android Settings. Tap the button below to open settings.
Select Numen
To use Numen, select it among the input methods. The next step lets you choose whether Numen should use a virtual keyboard or hardware-keyboard mode.
Pick the keyboard surface Numen should use here.
Titan 2 devices can show an extra IME caption bar under Numen. This OEM setting hides it and keeps Numen compact.
After: compact Numen

To get the most out of Numen, set the Fn key to act as Ctrl from Android system settings. Numen can show modifier state in the bottom strip, menu bar, or keyboard bar: active one-shot states use the active color, locked states use the locked color.
Mappings can also handle app shortcuts, media controls, Escape, Tab, Page Up/Down, and the compact bar.

This feature requires Shizuku to access trackpad events.

1. Install Shizuku from GitHub releases
2. Enable developer options in Android settings
3. Plug your device into a PC with ADB installed
4. Run the command that Shizuku shows in its app
5. Grant permission to Numen in Shizuku

The feature will work automatically once Shizuku is running.
